# Unified DNS in the Hybrid Multi-Cloud {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**[Download this whitepaper as DOCX](infoblox-hybrid-dns-unified-ddi.docx)** — a
Word copy of this page, regenerated on every site deploy. (Also available from
the **Other Formats** link in the page sidebar.)
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## In this whitepaper

Most hybrid DNS conversations begin at the wrong layer. They start with the
question of *which resolver to use* — Route 53, Azure Private DNS, Infoblox NIOS,
or a CSP-native service — when the real question is *who holds the policy plane*
and *what happens when that plane is split across five consoles that do not
synchronize*.

This paper makes three arguments. First: the traditional model of managing
per-CSP DNS independently — one team for Route 53, another for Azure Private DNS,
a third for GCP Cloud DNS — produces a class of failure called **split-brain DNS**
that is structurally impossible to eliminate without a unified control plane.
Second: Infoblox Universal DDI is that unified control plane, and its architecture
is well-documented — but the documentation stops short of the SD-WAN layer.
Third: **Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN**, the only Microsoft-certified partner for
Informed Network Routing (INR), intercepts DNS queries at the branch in ways that
interact with the Infoblox resolution chain in a manner neither vendor currently
documents. That interaction — and a critical scoping boundary that makes INR
irrelevant to GCC Moderate, GCC High, and DoD tenants — is the subject of
the second half of this paper.

The reference architecture in Part 5 does not exist in any Infoblox or Cisco
publication. It is synthesized here from first principles, vendor documentation,
and RFC-level DNS forwarder behavior.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Scope boundary — Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN only

This paper addresses SD-WAN DNS interception exclusively in the context of
**Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (IOS XE SD-WAN ≥ 20.4/17.4)**, which as of the
Microsoft Learn INR documentation (updated 2026-03-10) is the only SD-WAN
vendor listed in the INR "Currently enabled solutions" table. No other SD-WAN
vendor is covered.
:::

## Part 1 — The Broken Promise of Per-CSP DNS Sync

### 1.1 How organizations arrive at three DNS consoles

No organization sets out to manage DNS in three places. The fragmentation is
an emergent property of cloud adoption: when the first workload moved to AWS,
the team adopted Route 53 because it is native, well-integrated, and requires
no additional licensing. When Azure arrived, Azure Private DNS was the natural
companion to Azure Private Endpoints. When GCP joined the estate, Cloud DNS
followed. Each decision was locally rational. The aggregate result is an
organization whose DNS policy lives in three independent systems that were
never designed to share state.

The operational surface this produces is significant. Each CSP DNS system has
its own console, its own API, its own zone model, its own conditional forwarding
syntax, and its own behavior under failure. An engineer who knows Route 53
Resolver rules fluently must relearn the equivalent construct in Azure (Private
DNS zones linked to virtual networks via DNS zone links) and again in GCP
(Cloud DNS private zones with inbound server policies). The *concepts* translate;
the *mechanics* do not.

On-premises DNS — typically Infoblox NIOS or Windows Server DNS — sits alongside
these three systems, not above them. It can forward to CSP resolvers, and CSP
resolvers can forward queries back, but the forwarding topology must be manually
configured and manually maintained on every participating system. There is no
shared policy object, no shared zone propagation mechanism, and no authoritative
record of what the intended resolution path is for any given namespace.

### 1.2 Split-brain DNS: the failure mode that scales with complexity

Split-brain DNS is what you get when the answer to a DNS query depends on
*where the query originates*, not on what the intended answer is.

In a per-CSP model, split-brain is structurally guaranteed. Consider a private
endpoint for an Azure Storage account. Azure Private DNS resolves
`storageaccount.blob.core.windows.net` to a RFC 1918 address — say,
`10.0.1.50` — when the query arrives from within the virtual network. The same
query from on-premises resolves to a public IP unless the on-premises DNS
server has been explicitly configured to forward `.blob.core.windows.net`
queries to the Azure Private DNS resolver, *and* that forwarding rule is kept
current as endpoints are added, removed, or re-homed to different virtual
networks.

![The per-CSP DNS failure modes: split-brain (resolution diverges by query origin), sync lag (private zone changes propagate with delay), and policy drift (three consoles enforce three independent security postures with no reconciliation)](images/infoblox-hybrid-dns-diagram-01-per-csp-failure.png){#fig-per-csp-failure fig-alt="Blueprint diagram on a white background. Three vertical lanes labeled Route 53, Azure Private DNS, and GCP Cloud DNS, each with a console icon and an independent lock icon showing separate security policies. A central on-premises NIOS box below shows arrows pointing up to each lane with red dashed connectors labeled manual forwarding rules. Three red failure callout boxes: SPLIT-BRAIN — same query resolves to RFC 1918 from inside CSP, resolves to public IP from on-prem when forwarding lags; SYNC LAG — private zone change takes minutes to propagate across manual forwarding topology; POLICY DRIFT — RPZ rule added in on-prem does not automatically apply in Route 53 or Azure DNS. Navy background boxes for the CSP lanes, teal for NIOS, red for failure callouts. White background overall. Federal navy #1F3A5F, teal #1A9E8F, amber #D4860B, red #C0392B." width="100%"}

The failure this produces is insidious because it is intermittent. A workload
running on an EC2 instance in AWS correctly resolves the Azure private endpoint
only if the Route 53 Resolver outbound rule is configured, current, and
forwarding to the correct Azure Private Resolver IP. If the Azure private
endpoint is deprovisioned and a new one is created at a different IP, the
Route 53 rule must be updated. That update is manual. Until it is made, the
old IP answers — or the query fails — and the failure appears at the
application layer, not the DNS layer, because the DNS response itself may look
correct (an RFC 1918 address is returned) while routing to the wrong host.

Infoblox's multi-cloud solutions page states the core problem directly:
*"Siloed DNS, IP address management, security and policy across public clouds
hinder control over IP spaces and global policy enforcement, raising security
risks."* The paper's argument is more specific: the problem is not merely
operational friction. The problem is that the traditional model makes a
*consistent* security posture structurally impossible, because policy must be
replicated by hand to every participating DNS system and the replication has
no enforcement mechanism.

### 1.3 Policy fragmentation across three consoles

DNS security policy — Response Policy Zones (RPZ), DNS Firewall rules, DNSSEC
validation chains — is not portable across CSP DNS systems. An RPZ block
list maintained in Infoblox NIOS applies only to queries that reach NIOS.
Queries that are forwarded directly to Route 53 by a workload on an EC2
instance bypass the RPZ entirely. AWS Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall has its
own rule syntax, its own domain list management, and its own logging output.
Azure DNS Private Resolver has no equivalent RPZ mechanism; security policy
there is enforced at the network layer, not the DNS layer.

The practical consequence: an organization that believes it has a unified
DNS security posture because its on-premises NIOS cluster is running RPZ
actually has a security posture that applies only to queries that reach
NIOS — and in a hybrid multi-cloud estate, a significant fraction of queries
never do.

## Part 2 — Infoblox Universal DDI: One Control Plane Across Every Surface

### 2.1 What Universal DDI is

Infoblox Universal DDI is a SaaS management plane that provides a single
console and API for DNS, DHCP, and IP address management (DDI) across a
heterogeneous estate. As of the November 2025 / January 2026 feature release,
the management plane covers:

- **On-premises:** Infoblox NIOS, Infoblox NIOS-X, Microsoft Windows Server DNS
- **AWS:** Amazon Route 53
- **Azure:** Microsoft Azure DNS (with documented integration limitations noted below)
- **GCP:** Google Cloud DNS
- **Edge and CDN:** Cloudflare, Akamai

The Cloudflare and Akamai integrations were added in late 2025, confirmed by
Network World's November 2025 coverage of the Universal DDI platform expansion.
The current integration list should be verified against the Infoblox Universal
DDI product page before publication, as integrations are actively evolving.

![Infoblox Universal DDI as a single SaaS management plane spanning on-premises NIOS and NIOS-X, all three major CSPs, and edge providers — one console, one API, one policy object propagated to every DNS surface](images/infoblox-hybrid-dns-diagram-02-universal-ddi-plane.png){#fig-universal-ddi fig-alt="Architecture diagram on a white background. At the top center, a large teal rounded rectangle labeled INFOBLOX UNIVERSAL DDI — SaaS Management Plane — single console, single API, unified policy. Below it, seven boxes arranged in two rows connected by solid teal lines downward: Row 1 — on-premises: NIOS grid (navy), NIOS-X (navy), Windows Server DNS (navy); Row 2 — cloud: Amazon Route 53 (amber outline), Microsoft Azure DNS (amber outline, dagger note: integration limitations documented), Google Cloud DNS (amber outline), Cloudflare and Akamai (teal outline, labeled edge/CDN, added Nov 2025). A horizontal red dashed line below the management plane labeled WITHOUT UNIVERSAL DDI — separate console per surface, manual policy replication, no reconciliation. Caption: one policy object propagated down to every DNS surface simultaneously. White background. Federal navy #1F3A5F, teal #1A9E8F, amber #D4860B." width="100%"}

The key architectural distinction is that Universal DDI does not replace
per-CSP DNS services — Route 53 still serves Route 53 zones, Azure Private
DNS still serves Azure private zones. What Universal DDI replaces is the
*management layer* above them: the console, the API, and the policy object.
An RPZ block configured in Universal DDI propagates to every managed surface
simultaneously. An IP address assignment made in the central IPAM feeds the
correct zone on the correct CSP without manual reconciliation.

### 2.2 The Azure DNS integration caveat

Infoblox's technical documentation at `docs.infoblox.com` confirms the Azure
DNS integration with a noted limitation. The nature of that limitation — whether
it affects zone delegation, private endpoint resolution, or split-horizon
behavior — was not fetchable from the research pass and should be verified
directly in Infoblox's Azure DNS integration documentation before any
customer deployment conversation references Azure capabilities.

This is not a product deficiency unique to Infoblox. Azure Private DNS has
architectural constraints that affect every third-party DDI system: private
zones must be linked to virtual networks, resolution of private endpoint FQDNs
requires the query to arrive via the vnet-linked resolver, and cross-tenant
private DNS resolution requires additional Private Resolver forwarding
rulesets. Any integration operating across these constraints will have
documented limitations.

### 2.3 Why overlay management beats parallel management

The argument for Universal DDI is not merely that one console is more
convenient than three. The argument is that *policy consistency requires a
single source of truth for policy objects*, and no amount of process discipline
makes parallel management consistent — because the failure mode of parallel
management is silent. When an RPZ rule is updated in NIOS and the equivalent
Route 53 DNS Firewall rule is not, no alarm fires. The two systems diverge
quietly, and the divergence surfaces only when a DNS query is answered
differently depending on which resolver it reaches — which is, precisely,
split-brain DNS.

Universal DDI's single policy object eliminates the class of failures that
arise from policy replication lag, because the replication is automated and
the policy object itself is authoritative. The question of whether the Route 53
surface has the current block list is answered by the management plane, not by
manual audit.

## Part 3 — Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN DNS Interception: What the Vendors Don't Explain

### 3.1 The gap in vendor documentation

Neither Infoblox nor Cisco has published documentation explaining how Cisco
Catalyst SD-WAN DNS interception interacts with a Infoblox DDI resolution
chain. The Infoblox Universal DDI product page contains a single generic
bullet — "Optimize SD-WAN" — with no technical detail. The Cisco INR blog
covers URL categorization and traffic steering at a marketing level and
contains no DNS interception mechanics, no resolution flow architecture, and
no analysis of how interception affects DDI policy enforcement.

The Infoblox SD-WAN solutions page (`infoblox.com/solutions/sd-wan/`) and a
DDI-for-SD-WAN PDF exist, but they do not address the specific interaction
with Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN's `redirect-dns` policy mechanism and its
interaction with the NIOS/BloxOne forwarder. This section authors that
interaction from first principles.

### 3.2 How Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN intercepts DNS

Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (IOS XE SD-WAN) implements DNS interception through its
`redirect-dns` data policy feature. When a branch device sends a DNS query,
the SD-WAN edge router can be configured to intercept that query — regardless
of its configured resolver — and redirect it to a designated DNS server,
typically a Cisco Umbrella DNS resolver for DNS-layer security enforcement,
or a local Infoblox BloxOne endpoint.

The interception operates at Layer 7: the SD-WAN router acts as a transparent
DNS proxy. A query sent by a workstation to `8.8.8.8:53` is intercepted and
forwarded to the policy-designated resolver instead. The originating workstation
receives a response indistinguishable from a native response; it is unaware that
its resolver was redirected.

This mechanism has a critical interaction with the Infoblox resolution chain:
**the interception point determines whether Infoblox DDI policy is applied.**

### 3.3 The resolution chain and where policy enforcement lives

In a standard Infoblox deployment at an SD-WAN branch, the resolution chain
is intended to be:

```
Workstation → Branch Infoblox BloxOne Endpoint (or NIOS forwarder)
  → BloxOne DDI (SaaS, policy enforcement, RPZ, DNSSEC)
    → Recursive resolution (or per-CSP private resolver)
```

When Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN `redirect-dns` is active, the chain becomes:

```
Workstation → SD-WAN edge (intercepts UDP/TCP 53)
  → Policy-designated resolver (Umbrella, or NIOS, depending on policy)
    → [If NIOS: BloxOne DDI → recursive]
    → [If Umbrella: Cisco security stack → recursive]
```

![The Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN DNS interception chain: query origin, SD-WAN intercept point, and which path reaches Infoblox BloxOne DDI policy enforcement versus which path bypasses it entirely](images/infoblox-hybrid-dns-diagram-03-sdwan-interception-chain.png){#fig-sdwan-chain fig-alt="Left-to-right flow diagram on a white background. Far left: workstation icon labeled Branch User, arrow right to SD-WAN Edge Router box (Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, IOS XE 20.4+) with a red INTERCEPT band across it labeled redirect-dns policy. From the intercept, two paths fork downward: Path A (teal) labeled redirect to Infoblox BloxOne Endpoint goes to a BloxOne box then up to BloxOne DDI SaaS (RPZ enforced, DNSSEC validated, policy applied) then to CSP Private Resolver; Path B (red) labeled redirect to Cisco Umbrella goes to Umbrella DNS Security box then directly to recursive resolution, bypassing Infoblox DDI entirely. A red callout box on Path B reads: RPZ, DNSSEC validation, and IPAM policy from Universal DDI do NOT apply on this path. At the far right, a green box shows Per-CSP Private Zone (Route 53, Azure DNS, GCP Cloud DNS). Caption: the redirect-dns destination determines whether Universal DDI policy is enforced. White background, navy #1F3A5F, teal #1A9E8F, red #C0392B." width="100%"}

The policy consequence: if `redirect-dns` forwards to Cisco Umbrella, the
Infoblox DDI policy plane — RPZ enforcement, DNSSEC validation, NXDOMAIN
returns for blocked domains — is bypassed for every query that traverses that
path. The query reaches a CSP recursive resolver without passing through the
Infoblox control plane. From the Infoblox management console, this query is
invisible: no log entry, no policy evaluation, no block-list check.

If `redirect-dns` forwards to a local Infoblox BloxOne Endpoint (or a NIOS
forwarder), the DDI policy chain is preserved. The query enters the Infoblox
control plane, policy is evaluated, and the recursive resolution continues
through the BloxOne DDI SaaS plane.

### 3.4 INR telemetry and DNS query visibility

Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN's INR integration with Microsoft 365 operates by
collecting telemetry about M365-destined traffic flows and sharing that
telemetry with the Microsoft 365 Network Connectivity service. Microsoft
returns routing recommendations — which SD-WAN tunnel or exit point produces
the best M365 performance — and the SD-WAN policy is adjusted accordingly.

INR telemetry is gathered at the traffic-flow level, not the DNS query level.
The SD-WAN router observes the destination IP and port of M365-bound flows
(after DNS resolution has already occurred) and reports that data to Microsoft.
DNS interception and INR telemetry collection are therefore independent
mechanisms that can coexist. However, the interaction has one edge: if
`redirect-dns` is redirecting DNS to Umbrella, and Umbrella returns a
different M365 anycast IP than Infoblox NIOS would have returned (due to
different ECS subnet tagging or different anycast selection), the INR telemetry
Microsoft receives reflects the Umbrella-selected IP, not the
Infoblox-selected IP. In a split deployment — some queries through Umbrella,
some through NIOS — M365 telemetry will reflect a mixed population of query
paths, and Microsoft's routing recommendations may be suboptimal.

### 3.5 DNSSEC validation and the forwarder position problem

DNSSEC validation in a forwarder chain requires that the validating resolver
sit at or above the position where the query is first resolved. If Infoblox
BloxOne DDI is configured as a DNSSEC-validating resolver, it must be the
*first* resolver in the chain that performs recursion — not a forwarder that
receives a pre-resolved answer.

When Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN `redirect-dns` forwards a query to Umbrella, and
Umbrella performs recursive resolution and returns a validated response, DNSSEC
validation has occurred at the Umbrella layer. The BloxOne DDI control plane
has not validated anything, because the query never reached it. From a
compliance posture that requires DNSSEC validation to occur within the
organization's own control plane — a requirement that some federal frameworks
impose — a Umbrella-first `redirect-dns` configuration is non-compliant
regardless of Umbrella's own DNSSEC capabilities.

The correct configuration for environments where Infoblox Universal DDI is
the authoritative DDI control plane: `redirect-dns` must point to the local
Infoblox BloxOne Endpoint, not to Umbrella or any resolver outside the
Infoblox control plane. Umbrella (if in use for DNS security) should be
configured as a secondary path *within* the Infoblox forwarding chain, not
as the primary `redirect-dns` destination.

## Part 4 — The Federal Gap: INR Is Not Available in Sovereign Cloud

### 4.1 What INR is and why it matters

Microsoft 365 Informed Network Routing (INR) is a capability that allows
network equipment — specifically, certified SD-WAN devices — to share
traffic quality telemetry with Microsoft and receive per-service routing
recommendations in return. For Microsoft Teams and SharePoint, this produces
meaningful latency improvements: the SD-WAN device routes M365 traffic through
the tunnel or exit point that Microsoft has determined produces the best
performance for that specific tenant and time of day, rather than routing
by static policy.

Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (IOS XE SD-WAN ≥ 20.4/17.4) is the only SD-WAN
solution listed in the Microsoft Learn INR "Currently enabled solutions"
table as of the documentation's 2026-03-10 update. No other vendor appears
in that table.

### 4.2 The sovereign cloud exclusion

Microsoft 365 INR is explicitly scoped to WW Commercial cloud tenants.
Microsoft Learn states verbatim:

> *"Microsoft 365 informed network routing supports tenants in WW Commercial
> cloud but not the GCC Moderate, GCC High, DoD, Germany, or China clouds."*

This is not a temporary limitation or a gap in the roadmap — it reflects
the architectural boundary of INR, which depends on Microsoft's commercial
network telemetry infrastructure. The sovereign cloud environments (GCC
Moderate, GCC High, DoD) operate on separate infrastructure that does not
participate in the INR telemetry exchange.

![Federal sovereign cloud INR exclusion: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN INR applies only to WW Commercial tenants — GCC Moderate, GCC High, and DoD are explicitly excluded, and no published alternative achieves equivalent M365 traffic optimization for federal customers](images/infoblox-hybrid-dns-diagram-04-federal-inr-gap.png){#fig-federal-inr-gap fig-alt="Two-column comparison diagram on a white background. Left column header: WW COMMERCIAL (green check badge). Shows Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN router connected by teal arrows to Microsoft 365 INR telemetry exchange, which returns routing recommendations. M365 services (Teams, SharePoint, Exchange) shown with optimized routing paths. Right column header: GCC MODERATE / GCC HIGH / DoD (red X badge). Shows same Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN router with a red blocked line across the INR telemetry path labeled EXCLUDED — sovereign cloud boundary. M365 GCC services shown with static routing only, no telemetry feedback loop. Red callout: INR not available — no published Microsoft alternative for federal tenants. Caption from Microsoft Learn 2026-03-10: INR supports WW Commercial cloud but not GCC Moderate, GCC High, DoD, Germany, or China clouds. White background, navy #1F3A5F, teal #1A9E8F, red #C0392B, green #27AE60." width="100%"}

### 4.3 What federal Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN customers can use instead

Federal organizations running Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN in GCC Moderate, GCC High,
or DoD environments do not lose SD-WAN capabilities — they lose the INR
telemetry loop specifically. The following mechanisms remain available and
provide partial equivalence:

**Direct internet breakout with DSCP marking.** Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN can
identify M365-destined traffic by IP range (using Microsoft's published M365
endpoint lists) and route it via direct internet breakout rather than through
the MPLS backhaul. DSCP marking ensures QoS is preserved through the breakout
path. This is the recommended pattern in Microsoft's network connectivity
principles and remains fully available in sovereign cloud environments.

**Application-aware routing policies.** Cisco SD-WAN's application-aware
routing can measure real-time path quality metrics (latency, jitter, packet
loss) on SD-WAN tunnels and select the best path based on those measurements.
Without INR, the selection is made on locally observed metrics rather than
Microsoft-provided telemetry, which means the policy does not benefit from
Microsoft's visibility into its own network. The gap is real but bounded:
local measurement is operationally sound; INR provides an incremental
improvement by incorporating server-side telemetry.

**Infoblox DDI in the federal context.** The absence of INR does not affect
the Infoblox Universal DDI control plane. DNS resolution, RPZ enforcement,
DNSSEC validation, and IPAM management operate identically in GCC environments.
The `redirect-dns` configuration guidance in Part 3 applies equally to
federal Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN deployments: `redirect-dns` must point to the
BloxOne Endpoint to preserve Universal DDI policy enforcement, regardless of
whether INR is available.

## Part 5 — Reference Architecture

### 5.1 The end-to-end resolution flow (net-new)

This reference architecture synthesizes the components addressed in Parts 1–4
into a single end-to-end DNS resolution flow for a hybrid multi-cloud
environment with Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN branches. It does not exist in any
Infoblox or Cisco publication as of June 2026.

![End-to-end reference architecture: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN branch to Infoblox Universal DDI to per-CSP private zones — the complete DNS resolution flow that neither Infoblox nor Cisco has published](images/infoblox-hybrid-dns-diagram-05-reference-architecture.png){#fig-reference-arch fig-alt="Comprehensive left-to-right architecture diagram on a white background. Three zones separated by vertical dashed navy lines. Zone 1 labeled BRANCH (SD-WAN). Contains workstation icon, arrow to Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN edge router (IOS XE 20.4+) with redirect-dns label, arrow to BloxOne Endpoint (local DNS listener). Zone 2 labeled INFOBLOX UNIVERSAL DDI CONTROL PLANE (SaaS). Contains BloxOne DDI box (teal, large) with three internal function blocks: RPZ Enforcement, DNSSEC Validation, IPAM Policy. Teal arrows connect from BloxOne Endpoint inbound and from BloxOne DDI outbound to Zone 3. Zone 3 labeled PER-CSP PRIVATE RESOLUTION. Contains three stacked boxes: Amazon Route 53 Resolver with private zone, Microsoft Azure Private DNS Resolver with private zone, Google Cloud DNS with private zone. A red dashed bypass arrow from SD-WAN to Cisco Umbrella (outside the Infoblox plane) labeled AVOID — redirect-dns to Umbrella bypasses Universal DDI policy. Top-right corner callout: INR telemetry path (WW Commercial only) — dashed amber line from SD-WAN edge to Microsoft 365 INR service, labeled NOT AVAILABLE in GCC/DoD sovereign cloud. Caption: the correct configuration routes all branch DNS through BloxOne Endpoint so Universal DDI policy is evaluated before any per-CSP resolution. White background, navy #1F3A5F, teal #1A9E8F, amber #D4860B, red #C0392B." width="100%"}

### 5.2 Configuration requirements

The reference architecture depends on three configuration decisions being made
correctly. Each has a failure mode that produces a silent degradation of the
Universal DDI policy plane.

**Decision 1 — redirect-dns destination.** The Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN
`redirect-dns` data policy must designate the local Infoblox BloxOne Endpoint
(or NIOS forwarder) as the redirect target. Designating Cisco Umbrella or any
public resolver as the redirect target bypasses Universal DDI entirely for
all queries that traverse SD-WAN branches.

**Decision 2 — forwarding chain order.** If Umbrella is in use for
DNS-layer security alongside Infoblox DDI, Umbrella must be configured as
a *downstream* forwarder in the BloxOne DDI forwarding chain — not as an
upstream redirect target. The sequence must be:
`BloxOne Endpoint → BloxOne DDI (policy) → Umbrella (if used) → recursive`.
Reversing this order removes Infoblox policy from the enforcement path.

**Decision 3 — per-CSP conditional forwarding.** Universal DDI must hold
authoritative conditional forwarding rules for all private namespaces
(Azure private endpoint FQDNs, Route 53 private hosted zone names, GCP
internal service names). If these forwarding rules are maintained only in
on-premises NIOS and not synchronized to Universal DDI, branch queries that
enter via BloxOne Endpoint will not benefit from per-CSP private resolution
and will fall through to public recursive resolution — producing the same
split-brain behavior as the unmanaged per-CSP model.

### 5.3 Commercial versus federal deployment differences

The reference architecture is identical for WW Commercial and federal sovereign
cloud deployments, with one exception: the INR telemetry path in the upper
right of the diagram is present for commercial and absent for federal.

| Component | WW Commercial | GCC Moderate / GCC High / DoD |
|---|:--:|:--:|
| Infoblox Universal DDI | ✅ Full | ✅ Full |
| BloxOne Endpoint at SD-WAN branch | ✅ | ✅ |
| Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN redirect-dns | ✅ | ✅ |
| RPZ / DNSSEC via Universal DDI | ✅ | ✅ |
| Cisco SD-WAN INR telemetry loop | ✅ Available | ❌ Excluded |
| M365 optimization via DSCP / direct breakout | ✅ | ✅ (primary mechanism) |
| Application-aware routing (local metrics) | ✅ | ✅ |

For federal customers: the Infoblox DDI story is unchanged. The SD-WAN DNS
interception guidance is unchanged. The only missing piece is the INR
telemetry loop, which is replaced by DSCP-marked direct breakout and
application-aware routing on locally observed metrics.

## Appendix B — Open Questions for Vendor Engagement

Before customer publication, the following questions should be answered by
direct engagement with Infoblox and Cisco technical teams, as neither vendor
has published authoritative answers:

1. **Infoblox:** Does the BloxOne Cloud SD-WAN documentation contain technical
   detail on how `redirect-dns` interacts with BloxOne Endpoint? Specifically:
   does BloxOne Endpoint operate as a transparent DNS proxy that is compatible
   with SD-WAN redirect, or must the workstation be explicitly configured to
   use BloxOne Endpoint as its resolver?

2. **Infoblox:** What are the specific Azure DNS integration limitations noted
   in `docs.infoblox.com`? Do they affect private endpoint resolution, split-horizon
   zones, or conditional forwarding for Azure-managed FQDNs?

3. **Cisco:** When `redirect-dns` redirects a query to a BloxOne Endpoint,
   does the source IP presented to BloxOne Endpoint reflect the originating
   workstation (for ECS subnet selection purposes) or the SD-WAN edge router
   IP? This affects per-subnet resolution policy and geographic IP address
   management accuracy.

4. **Microsoft:** Is there a roadmap for expanding INR support to GCC Moderate
   or GCC High tenants? Is there an alternative telemetry mechanism for
   sovereign cloud customers that achieves comparable M365 path optimization?
